# Erythema multiforme

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Emergency medicine > Dermatologic disorders > Erythema multiforme*

[Original Article Link](/library/Tk06MT)

---

## Summary

<u>Erythema</u> multiforme is a rare, acute <u>hypersensitivity reaction</u> most commonly triggered by the <u>herpes simplex virus</u> (<u>HSV</u>). Additional triggers include infections (e.g., <u>Mycoplasma pneumonia</u>) and certain medications and <u>vaccines</u>. <u>Erythema</u> multiforme typically occurs in adults between 20–40 years of age and manifests as a polymorphic <u>rash</u> that begins as <u>macules</u> and <u>papules</u> and develops into characteristic <u>target lesions</u>. The <u>rash</u> initially appears on the <u>dorsal</u> aspect of the hands and feet and extends proximally. In patients with moderate to severe <u>mucosal</u> involvement with or without systemic symptoms, the condition is defined as <u>erythema multiforme major</u>. Diagnosis is usually clinical, but <u>serology</u> and/or <u>skin biopsy</u> may be performed if there is diagnostic uncertainty or to determine the underlying cause. <u>Erythema</u> multiforme is usually <u>self-limited</u> and resolves spontaneously within a month; symptomatic treatment with <u>antihistamines</u>, and <u>topical steroids</u> is usually sufficient. Patients with <u>erythema multiforme major</u> may require <u>systemic glucocorticoids</u> and, in severe cases, <u>IV fluid therapy</u> and <u>specialized nutritional support</u>.

---

## Etiology

<u>Erythema</u> multiforme is a <u>type IV hypersensitivity reaction</u>; , which can be triggered by the following.




* Infections:  (most common): <u>herpes simplex virus</u> (<u>HSV</u>), <u>Mycoplasma pneumoniae</u>, <u>SARS-CoV-2</u>, and <u>fungal infections</u>  [[2]](/library/6OdjtJ0)

* Medications: : e.g., <u>barbiturates</u>, <u>phenytoin</u>; , <u>NSAIDs</u>, <u>antibiotics</u> (e.g., <u>penicillin</u> or other <u>beta-lactams</u>, <u>sulfonamides</u>)

* <u>Vaccines</u> (rare): e.g., after <u>diphtheria</u>, <u>tetanus</u>, <u>influenza</u>, <u>hepatitis B</u> <u>vaccination</u>





References:[[1]](/library/u7apnN)[[2]](/library/6OdjtJ0)[[3]](/library/v7aAnN)

---

## Clinical features

* <u>Rash</u>

* Acute onset with progression from <u>erythematous</u> <u>macules</u> to <u>papules</u> and <u>vesicles</u> to <u>target lesions</u>

* Target lesions

* Characteristic of <u>erythema</u> multiforme, appear a few days after the onset of <u>rash</u>, may be absent in some patients

* <u>Target lesions</u> have three zones: an inner dark red/brown zone, surrounded by a pale zone, and an outer <u>erythematous</u> ring.

* <u>Epithelial</u> <u>necrosis</u> is present in the inner zone

* May be asymptomatic or cause <u>pruritus</u> and painful burning

* <u>Nikolsky sign</u> is negative.

* Distribution

* Symmetrical distribution

* Affects backs of hands and feet first → spreads proximally and can affect the entire body, including palms and soles

* <u>Mucosal</u> involvement is characteristic of <u>erythema multiforme major</u> but may also occur in <u>erythema multiforme minor</u>.

| <br>Comparison of subtypes of <u>erythema</u> multiforme [[2]](/library/6OdjtJ0)[[4]](/library/OOdIsJ0)[[5]](/library/zldrzJ0)<br> |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Clinical feature | Erythema multiforme minor | <br>Erythema multiforme major [[2]](/library/6OdjtJ0)<br> |
| Cutaneous <u>target lesions</u> | <br>* Present, without <u>epidermal</u> detachment<br><br> | <br>* More extensive cutaneous <u>target lesions</u> with <u>epidermal</u> detachment affecting < 10% of the <u>total body surface area</u> (<u>TBSA</u>) [[1]](/library/u7apnN)<br><br> |
| <u>Mucosal</u> involvement | <br>* None or minimal (typically localized to oral <u>mucosa</u>)<br><br> | <br><br>* Painful <u>ulcers</u> of the oral (most common)<br><br>* Ocular and/or genital <u>mucosal</u> involvement<br><br><br> |
| Systemic symptoms | <br>* Usually absent<br><br> | <br>* <u>Fever</u>, <u>myalgia</u>, and/or <u>arthralgia</u><br><br> |

---

## Diagnosis

<u>Erythema</u> multiforme is primarily a <u>clinical diagnosis</u> based on the presence of typical lesions (e.g., <u>target lesions</u>) and <u>patient history</u> (e.g., exposure, recent infection). [[4]](/library/OOdIsJ0)




### <u>Laboratory studies</u> [[6]](/library/lOdvsJ0)




* Routine studies: Obtain in patients with <u>erythema multiforme major</u>; the following findings may be seen.

* <u>Inflammatory markers</u> (e.g., ↑ <u>WBC</u>, ↑ <u>ESR</u>)

* ↑ <u>Liver</u> enzymes

* <u>Electrolyte</u> abnormalities (e.g., due to insufficient intake of liquids and/or food)

* Infectious disease workup: based on clinical suspicion

* <u>Diagnosis of herpes simplex infection</u>

* <u>M. pneumoniae</u> <u>serology</u> or <u>PCR</u>

* <u>COVID-19 testing</u>

* Additional studies: Consider if there is diagnostic uncertainty to determine underlying causes and exclude other conditions. [[4]](/library/OOdIsJ0)[[6]](/library/lOdvsJ0)

* Autoimmune studies, e.g.:

* <u>Antinuclear antibody</u> in suspected <u>lupus</u> erythematosus (<u>Rowell syndrome</u>)

* Serum complements in persistent <u>erythema</u> multiforme

* <u>Malignancy</u> workup (e.g., <u>leukemia</u>, <u>lymphoma</u>, solid organ <u>neoplasms</u>): especially in patients with recurrent <u>erythema</u> multiforme  [[6]](/library/lOdvsJ0)





### <u>Skin biopsy</u> [[6]](/library/lOdvsJ0)




* Indication: Consider if there is diagnostic uncertainty.

* Supportive findings (nonspecific)

* Evidence of inflammation (e.g., lymphohistiocytic infiltrate)

* <u>Necrotic</u> <u>keratinocytes</u>

* <u>Edema</u>

* Specific testing: Consider based on clinical suspicion.

* <u>Autoimmune blistering diseases</u>: <u>direct fluorescent antibody test</u>

* <u>HSV infections</u>: <u>Tzanck smear</u> test or <u>PCR</u>

---

## Differential diagnoses

* <u>Stevens-Johnson syndrome</u>: In comparison to <u>erythema</u> multiforme, <u>skin</u> involvement in <u>SJS</u> is more severe and usually triggered by medications.

* <u>Urticaria</u>: The lesions of <u>urticaria</u> are transient, disappearing within a few hours, while those of <u>erythema</u> multiforme last up to a month; <u>target lesions</u> are uncommon.

* <u>Prodrome</u> phase of <u>bullous pemphigoid</u>: <u>Prodromal</u> <u>rash</u> resembles that of <u>urticaria</u>/<u>erythema</u> multiforme; oral involvement is rare.

* Fixed drug eruption

* Definition: <u>hypersensitivity reaction</u> to specific drugs occurring within 8 hours of exposure

* Clinical features

* Well-defined, <u>erythematous</u>, pruritic lesions (often solitary)

* Oral <u>mucosa</u> may be affected; atypical <u>target lesions</u> may be present

* Resolves spontaneously on stopping the offending drug; may cause <u>postinflammatory hyperpigmentation</u>

* Diagnosis: provocation tests (oral challenge test/<u>skin patch</u> test)

* <u>Rowell syndrome</u>

* See also:

* “<u>Overview of annular skin lesions</u>”

* “<u>Maculopapular rashes</u>”

* “<u>Diffuse erythematous rashes</u>”

## Treatment

### General principles [[4]](/library/OOdIsJ0)[[6]](/library/lOdvsJ0)




* Treatment is primarily symptomatic.

* Discontinue any offending medications.

* Consider treating any underlying infection (e.g., <u>treatment of HSV infection</u>, <u>antibiotic therapy</u> for M. pneumonie).

* Consider <u>systemic glucocorticoid</u> therapy.

* For patients with <u>erythema multiforme major</u> with severe <u>mucosal</u> involvement, consider:

* <u>IV fluid therapy</u> and <u>electrolyte repletion</u> (management is similar to that of extensive <u>burns</u>)

* <u>Specialized nutrition support</u>

* <u>Antibiotic therapy for SSTIs</u>

* Specialist consultation (e.g., <u>ICU</u>, dermatology, ophthalmology)





> [!WARNING]
> Patients with <u>erythema multiforme major</u> and severe oral <u>mucosal</u> involvement may suffer from <u>dehydration</u> and/or <u>electrolyte</u> abnormalities due to insufficient intake of liquids and food. [[6]](/library/lOdvsJ0)




> [!TIP]
> Most patients with <u>erythema multiforme minor</u> require no specific treatment because the condition is <u>self-limited</u>. [[4]](/library/OOdIsJ0)




### Pharmacotherapy [[2]](/library/6OdjtJ0)[[4]](/library/OOdIsJ0)[[6]](/library/lOdvsJ0)




#### <u>Antiviral therapy</u>




* Acute <u>erythema</u> multiforme episode: Consider antiviral <u>treatment of HSV infection</u> (uncertain benefit).  [[2]](/library/6OdjtJ0)[[4]](/library/OOdIsJ0)[[6]](/library/lOdvsJ0)

* Recurrent <u>erythema</u> multiforme: Long-term antiviral suppression therapy (e.g., <u>acyclovir</u> (<u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE for 6 months) is recommended as prophylaxis.





> [!TIP]
> Pharmacotherapy (e.g., antivirals, <u>systemic glucocorticoids</u>) is recommended in patients with recurrent <u>erythema</u> multiforme to prevent further episodes. [[4]](/library/OOdIsJ0)[[6]](/library/lOdvsJ0)




#### <u>Supportive care</u> [[2]](/library/6OdjtJ0)




* <u>Systemic glucocorticoids</u>

* Consider in patients with <u>erythema multiforme major</u> with severe <u>mucosal</u> involvement.  [[2]](/library/6OdjtJ0)[[4]](/library/OOdIsJ0)[[6]](/library/lOdvsJ0)

* Example agent: <u>prednisone</u> DOSAGE with a prolonged taper over 2–4 weeks [[2]](/library/6OdjtJ0)[[6]](/library/lOdvsJ0)

* Topical <u>glucocorticoids</u> (e.g., <u>hydrocortisone</u> DOSAGE)

* <u>Antihistamines</u> for <u>pruritus</u> (e.g., <u>hydroxyzine</u> DOSAGE)

* <u>Mucosal</u> care, e.g.: [[2]](/library/6OdjtJ0)

* Oral <u>anesthetics</u>, <u>antiseptic</u> solution, and/or high-<u>potency</u> <u>hydrocortisone</u> gel

* Ophthalmology consultation and ophthalmic medications (e.g., topical lubricants)

* <u>Pain management</u>: See “<u>Oral analgesics</u>” and “<u>Parenteral analgesics</u>” for dosages.
